meta.title: Password365 — Password manager without cloud or account
meta.description: Password365 (Password 365) is an open-source password manager with no cloud and no account. Passwords, passkeys and one-time codes stay on your devices and sync directly, 365 days a year.

hero.eyebrow: Synced across your devices. Stored on no one else's.
hero.title: Not your server, not your passwords.
hero.lead: Password365 keeps your passwords, passkeys and one-time codes in sync across your computer, phone and tablet — without ever putting them on a server you don't control. No account, no cloud.
hero.note: Free for Mac, Windows and Linux. iPhone and iPad coming soon. Android in development.

why.title: Why not the cloud?
why.lead: Cloud password managers encrypt your vault too. But they keep it — and millions of others — on their servers.

target.title: One target, millions of vaults
target.text: A server holding everyone's encrypted vaults is worth attacking. When one is breached, attackers take the vaults with them and can keep guessing at the passwords for as long as they like.

control.title: Your copy, your rules
control.text: With Password365 your vault lives only on your devices, kept in sync between them. There is no copy on anyone else's server to steal, leak or lose access to.

offline.title: Works without the internet
offline.text: No outage, no lost account and no change of terms can lock you out of your own passwords.

why.quote: Crypto holders say: not your keys, not your coins. The same is true of passwords: if they live on someone else's server, they are only as safe as that server.

features.title: Everything a password manager should do
features.lead: The features you expect, on your own devices.

autofill.title: Fills in for you
autofill.text: Usernames, passwords and one-time codes filled in on websites and apps, from the browser extension and from AutoFill on iPhone and iPad.

passkeys.title: Passkeys
passkeys.text: Create and use passkeys on any site that supports them, and keep them with the rest of your logins.

totp.title: Two-factor codes built in
totp.text: Add the setup key once and Password365 shows the code, and fills it in together with your password.

watchtower.title: Watchtower
watchtower.text: Finds weak, reused and old passwords, and logins that could use two-factor authentication. Checked on your device.

categories.title: More than passwords
categories.text: Credit cards, identities, secure notes, bank accounts, passports, Wi-Fi, SSH keys, documents and more than 20 categories, with the right fields for your country.

generator.title: Strong passwords on demand
generator.text: Random passwords, easy-to-type passphrases and PINs, generated on the spot.

quickAccess.title: Quick Access
quickAccess.text: A keyboard shortcut opens your vault over any app on your computer: search, copy, done.

attachments.title: Files and documents
attachments.text: Attach scans and files to any item, encrypted like everything else.

ssh.title: For developers
ssh.text: An SSH agent for the keys in your vault, and auto-type for apps that do not accept filling.

sync.title: All your devices in sync. No cloud in between.
sync.lead: Not an offline vault you have to copy around: add as many computers, phones and tablets as you like and they keep each other up to date automatically. They talk directly, on your own network — your vault never goes through a server, ours or anyone else's.

step1.title: Pair once
step1.text: Scan a QR code shown on your computer with your iPhone. That is the whole setup.

step2.title: Change anywhere
step2.text: Add or edit items on any device. Each change is encrypted before it leaves the device.

step3.title: Stay in sync
step3.text: The next time both devices are on the same network, they exchange what changed. No account, no subscription to a cloud.

security.title: Encrypted before anything else happens
security.lead: Your vault is unlocked by two secrets: the master password you remember and a Secret Key that is created on your device and never leaves your hands.

keys.title: Two keys, not one
keys.text: Even someone with a copy of your vault file and a lucky guess at your password cannot open it without your Secret Key.

crypto.title: Modern, proven cryptography
crypto.text: Argon2id makes guessing your password slow and expensive. XChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts and authenticates every item.

local.title: Nothing to breach
local.text: There is no central server holding everyone's vaults, so there is no central server to break into.

migrate.title: Bring your passwords with you
migrate.lead: Import from your browser or your current password manager in a few clicks. Logins, cards, notes, passkeys and attachments come along where the export includes them.
migrate.others: and CSV or CXF files from other apps

faq.title: Questions
faq.q0: Is this an offline password manager where I copy the vault file myself?
faq.a0: No. Password365 syncs automatically between all your devices, like a cloud password manager does — the difference is that the devices talk to each other directly instead of through someone else's server. There are no files to move by hand.
faq.q1: What happens if I lose my phone?
faq.a1: Your vault is encrypted and locked with Face ID or Touch ID and your master password. Your items are still on your computer, and you can set up a new phone from it.
faq.q2: What if I forget my master password?
faq.a2: Nobody can reset it for you — that is what keeps your vault private. Keep your Emergency Kit (it has your Secret Key and room to write your password) somewhere safe, and back up your vault from the app.
faq.q3: Do I need to be on the same network to sync?
faq.a3: Yes. Devices sync when they can reach each other on the same network. In between, each device keeps working on its own with everything it has.
faq.q4: Does Password365 use the internet at all?
faq.a4: Only if you turn on the check for passwords found in data breaches (off by default). It sends the first 5 characters of a hash of each password, never the password itself.
faq.q5: Can I move my data out later?
faq.a5: Yes. Export everything to CSV or to the Credential Exchange Format (CXF), which other password managers can import, passkeys included.
faq.a6: Because your passwords are needed every day. Password365 is built to work 365 days a year: it keeps working offline, there is no account that can expire or be suspended, and no server whose outage can lock you out. You may also see the name written Password 365.

cta.title: Take your passwords back.
cta.text: Free on your computer. No account needed. Works 365 days a year, even offline.

download.title: Download Password365
download.lead: Start on your computer, then add your phone and your browser.
download.extensionText: For Chrome, Edge and Firefox. It works together with the app on your computer.
download.iosText: AutoFill, passkeys and Face ID, synced with your computer.

download.androidText: AutoFill in browsers and apps, synced with your computer.

steps.title: Install the app on your computer
steps.text: Open the installer for Mac, Windows or Linux. There is no account to create and no email to give.

steps.title: Create your vault
steps.text: Choose a master password. The app creates a Secret Key on your device and an Emergency Kit to print or save somewhere safe.

steps.title: Add your browser
steps.text: Install the extension for Chrome, Edge or Firefox. It works together with the app on your computer to fill in logins and passkeys.

steps.title: Add your phone
steps.text: Install the iPhone app and scan the QR code your computer shows. From then on, your devices keep each other up to date on your own network.

download.importText: Coming from another password manager? Bring your logins, cards, notes and passkeys with you.

faq.q: Is Password365 free?
faq.a: Free on computer and browser; the iPhone app is a subscription. There are no ads and no paid cloud plan, because there is no cloud.

faq.q: Do I need an account to use it?
faq.a: No. You download the app and create your vault on your own device. There is no sign-up, no email and no server that keeps your data.

faq.q: Where do the downloads come from?
faq.a: The computer installers and the extension are the files published with each release in the project's public GitHub repository, where the source code is too.

faq.q: Is the code open?
faq.a: Yes. Password365 is open source under the GPL-3.0 license, so anyone can read how your vault is encrypted and synced.

securityPage.title: Security
securityPage.lead: How Password365 protects your data, in plain words and in detail.
securityPage.p1: Your data is encrypted on your device before it is written anywhere.
securityPage.p2: Only you hold the keys. We never see your master password, your Secret Key or your items, and we cannot recover them.
securityPage.p3: Devices sync directly with each other. There is no Password365 server.
securityPage.p4: The only online features, the breached-password check and update checks, are off until you turn them on.
securityPage.unlock1: Your master password is stretched with Argon2id (256 MB of memory on computers, 128 MB on phones), which makes every guess slow and costly.
securityPage.unlock2: Your Secret Key — 128 random bits created on your device — is mixed in with HKDF-SHA-256. A copy of your vault cannot be attacked with password guesses alone.
securityPage.unlock3: After a few wrong passwords in a row, each new try has to wait longer.
securityPage.enc1: Every item is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305, with a random nonce each time. Any change to the encrypted data is detected and refused.
securityPage.enc2: Each encrypted record is bound to its vault, its item and its version, so records cannot be swapped or replayed.
securityPage.enc3: On iPhone, the vault file also gets the system's file protection, and Face ID unlock keeps its key in the Secure Enclave–protected Keychain, for 14 days at most before your master password is needed again.
securityPage.sync1: Pairing uses a QR code shown on your computer: the phone and the computer authenticate each other with it before anything is exchanged.
securityPage.sync2: Every sync runs over an end-to-end encrypted channel (the Noise protocol with X25519), on your local network.
securityPage.sync3: A device can be removed from your account at any time.
securityPage.data2: If you turn on the breached-password check, the first 5 characters of the SHA-1 hash of each password are sent to Have I Been Pwned, which answers with every matching hash (k-anonymity). The password never leaves your device.
securityPage.open1: The cryptography is written down in a detailed specification, with test vectors, and checked by automated tests on every change.

privacyPage.title: Privacy policy
privacyPage.intro: Password365 is built so that we do not have your data. This policy explains what that means in practice.
privacyPage.apps1: Password365 does not collect any data. There is no account and no sign-up. Your vault is created, encrypted and kept on your devices.
privacyPage.apps2: Devices sync directly with each other on your local network. Your data does not pass through any server of ours.
privacyPage.apps3: The apps contain no analytics, no advertising and no tracking of any kind.
privacyPage.apps4: If you turn on the breached-password check (off by default), the app sends the first 5 characters of a hash of each password to Have I Been Pwned (haveibeenpwned.com). It cannot learn your passwords from them.
privacyPage.store1: Apps downloaded from the App Store are delivered by Apple, and any purchase is processed by Apple under its own privacy policy. We do not receive your payment details.
privacyPage.site1: This website uses no cookies and no analytics. It is served by Cloudflare, which processes technical data such as IP addresses to deliver and protect it.
privacyPage.apps5: If you turn on update checks (the app asks the first time you open it), the desktop app asks GitHub (github.com), where Password365 is published, for the newest version once a day. GitHub sees the request, like any website visit; nothing about you or your vault is sent.

supportPage.title: Support
supportPage.contact: Write to {email}. Never send us your master password or your Secret Key — we will never ask for them.
supportPage.start1: Install Password365 on your computer and create your vault. Save the Emergency Kit it offers: it holds your Secret Key.
supportPage.start2: Import your passwords from your browser or your current password manager (Import, in the toolbar).
supportPage.start3: Install the browser extension to fill in and save logins.
supportPage.start4: On your iPhone, choose “Set up with another device” and scan the QR code shown on your computer, in Devices.
supportPage.recover1: You need your master password and your Secret Key. The Secret Key is on your Emergency Kit, and in Settings on any device that is still signed in.
supportPage.recover2: Nobody, including us, can reset your master password.
supportPage.discussText: Ask a question, share an idea or show what you built. Bugs go to Issues.

footer.tagline: The password manager without a cloud.

open.title: Open source, checked in the open
open.lead: You should not have to take our word for it. The core that holds and protects your passwords is public, and so are the desktop app and the browser extension: anyone can read them, build them and check what they do with your passwords.

code.title: Read the code
code.text: The core (cryptography, vault and sync), the desktop app and the browser extension are published on GitHub under the GPL-3.0 license: free to use, study and share. The iPhone and Android apps are built on that same core; the code of their screens is not published.

verify.title: Verify it
verify.text: The cryptography and the sync protocol are written down, with a threat model. Automated tests run on every change. It has not had an independent audit yet; we say so, and we welcome reviewers.

help.title: Help build it
help.text: Report a bug, suggest an idea, add your language or send a fix. Found a vulnerability? Report it privately and we will answer within 7 days.

noCloud.title: A password manager without the cloud
noCloud.teaser: What it means, how it stays safe, and what you give up.
noCloud.description: A password manager with no cloud and no account: your encrypted vault stays on your own devices, which sync directly. How it works, what it protects against, and its limits.
noCloud.lead: Most password managers keep a copy of your encrypted vault on their servers so your devices can stay in sync. A password manager without the cloud does the same job without that copy: the vault lives only on your devices.

p: There is no Password365 account and no Password365 server that holds your vault. You create the vault on your computer, protect it with a master password and a Secret Key, and add your phone and browser by pairing them with the computer.
Your devices then keep each other up to date directly, over your own network. Nothing about your passwords is sent to us.

ul: A server that stores millions of vaults is worth attacking. If it is breached, the attackers get encrypted vaults they can try to open for as long as they like. With no copy on a server, there is nothing to take.
No account to lose, no subscription that can lock you out of your own passwords, and no company whose outage, sale or change of terms affects you.
It keeps working with no internet connection.

p: Your vault is encrypted before it is saved, using your master password and a Secret Key generated on your device. Both are needed to open it. The code is open (GPL-3.0), and the cryptography and the sync protocol are written down, with a threat model.

One thing to be clear about: Password365 has not had an independent security audit yet. Established managers such as 1Password and Bitwarden have been audited and have years in the field. If an audit matters to you, that is a fair reason to wait.

ul: Syncing needs your devices to reach each other, which today means the same network. There is no sync over the internet.
No sharing with other people (family or team vaults) yet.
If you lose every device and your Emergency Kit, nobody can recover your vault, including us. Keep the Emergency Kit and back up your vault from the app.
The iPhone app is coming soon and Android is in development.

p: People who want control of their own data, work mostly on a computer or two and a phone, and prefer fewer moving parts. If you need to share passwords with a team, or sync over the internet from anywhere, a cloud manager fits better today.

faq.q: Does Password365 need an account?
faq.a: No. There is no account. You create a vault on your own device.

faq.q: Where is my vault stored?
faq.a: Only on your own devices, encrypted. There is no copy on a Password365 server.

faq.q: Can I still use it on my phone and in my browser?
faq.a: Yes. You pair the phone and the browser extension with your computer, and they keep each other in sync directly. The iPhone app is coming soon; Android is in development.

faq.q: What if I lose my computer?
faq.a: If another paired device still has your vault, you can set up a new one from it. Otherwise you need your Emergency Kit (it holds your Secret Key) and a backup of your vault.

alternative.title: Password365 vs 1Password and Bitwarden: an honest comparison
alternative.teaser: Where it differs from 1Password and Bitwarden, and where they are ahead.
alternative.description: Password365 compared with 1Password and Bitwarden: accounts, where the vault lives, sync, open source, audits and sharing. Where each one is the better choice.
alternative.lead: 1Password and Bitwarden are mature, widely trusted password managers. Password365 is newer and takes a different route: no account and no cloud. This page says where that matters and where they are simply ahead.

p: 1Password and Bitwarden keep your encrypted vault on their servers (Bitwarden also lets you host your own) and sync your devices through them. You need an account. Password365 has no account and no server: the vault stays on your devices, which sync directly with each other.

sections.h: Where Password365 may suit you better
ul: You do not want your encrypted vault on anyone else's server.
You want no account to create, no email to confirm, and nothing that can be suspended.
You want open code: the core, the desktop app and the browser extension are published under GPL-3.0 (1Password is closed source).
The computer and browser versions are free.
Independent security audits and years of public track record. Password365 has not had an audit yet.
Sharing with family and teams, and administration tools for companies.
Sync over the internet, from any network, and apps already on both phone stores.
Wider browser and platform coverage, and larger support teams.

p: If you share passwords with other people, need to sync from anywhere, or want an audited product today, choose 1Password or Bitwarden. If you want to keep the vault on your own devices and accept syncing on your network, try Password365. You can test it without leaving your current manager: Password365 imports 1Password and Bitwarden exports.

faq.q: Can I move from 1Password or Bitwarden?
faq.a: Yes. Password365 imports a 1Password export (1PUX), a Bitwarden export and a KeePass file, plus CSV files from browsers. See the import guide.

faq.q: Is Password365 as secure as 1Password or Bitwarden?
faq.a: We cannot claim that. It uses established cryptography and is open source, but it has not had an independent audit, and they have. Read the security page and the threat model, and decide.

faq.q: Can I use it alongside my current manager?
faq.a: Yes. Import a copy of your passwords to try it, and keep the other manager until you are sure.

importing.title: Import your passwords from 1Password, Bitwarden, Chrome and more
importing.teaser: Move your logins, cards, notes and passkeys in a few clicks.
importing.description: How to import passwords into Password365 from 1Password, Bitwarden, KeePass, Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge or a CSV or CXF file, and why to delete the export afterwards.
importing.lead: Password365 reads exports from the password managers and browsers most people use. Logins, cards, notes, passkeys and attachments come along where the export includes them.

ul: 1Password: an export file (.1pux)
Bitwarden: its exported file
KeePass and KeePassXC: a .kdbx database
Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari: the passwords CSV they export
Other apps: a CSV file, or a Credential Exchange (CXF) file, which can include passkeys
Export from your current app or browser. Look for Export in its settings and choose a format from the list above.
On your computer, open Password365 and choose Import in the toolbar. Pick the file.
Check the result screen: it tells you how many items were new and how many were already in your vault.
Your other devices need nothing: the imported items sync from the computer.

p: An export is a readable copy of your passwords. Delete it as soon as the import is done and empty the trash. Do not send it by email or leave it in a cloud folder.

ul: Duplicates: Password365 skips an item that is already in the vault. If the same account came from two sources, use Review duplicates in the sidebar to merge them.
Missing items: not every export includes every kind of item. Check what the source exported.

p: You can export everything from Password365 to CSV or to the Credential Exchange Format, so your data is never locked in.

faq.q: Is it safe to import?
faq.a: The import runs on your device and nothing is uploaded. The risk is the export file itself, so delete it afterwards.

faq.q: Can I import passkeys?
faq.a: Yes, through a Credential Exchange (CXF) file, or an export that includes them.

sync.title: How Password365 syncs without a server
sync.teaser: Pair once, then your devices update each other directly.
sync.description: How Password365 keeps your devices in sync with no cloud: pairing with a QR code, encrypted direct connections on your network, and what happens when devices are apart.
sync.lead: Password365 syncs your computer, phone and browser without a server in between. Devices find each other on your network, prove who they are, and exchange only what changed.

p: Pairing connects two devices. One shows a QR code and the other scans it with its camera (or you paste the code). The new device then shows six digits, which you type on the device that already has your vault. That check makes sure you are pairing your own device, not a stranger's on the same network.
The code works once and expires after five minutes.

ul: Every connection between paired devices is encrypted and authenticated (a modern secure-channel handshake), and each device only accepts devices it has paired with.
Your vault is already encrypted before it is saved, and changes are exchanged encrypted.
Nothing goes through our servers, because there are none for your vault.

p: Each device keeps working on its own with everything it has. The next time two paired devices can reach each other on the same network, they exchange what changed. If two devices changed the same item, the newest change is kept and the other password goes into the item's history.
You can also move changes with a sync file: save it on one device and open it on the other, for example by AirDrop. The file is for one specific paired device.

ul: Today devices must reach each other on the same network. There is no sync over the internet.
A new device needs a device that already has the vault to pair with.

faq.q: Do I need Wi-Fi?
faq.a: Your devices need to be on the same network to sync. Between syncs, each one works on its own, offline.

faq.q: Does anything go through your servers?
faq.a: No. We run no servers for your vault.

faq.q: What if I remove a device?
faq.a: Remove it in Devices. It is refused on the next sync and keeps only the copy it already had, protected by your master password.

keepass.title: Password365 vs KeePassXC: two ways to keep your passwords off the cloud
keepass.teaser: Both avoid a company cloud. How sync, phones and setup differ.
keepass.description: Password365 and KeePassXC both keep your passwords out of a company's cloud. How they differ in sync, phone apps, setup and features, and who each one suits.
keepass.lead: KeePassXC is a well-known open-source password manager that keeps your passwords in a file on your computer. Password365 shares the idea (no account, no company cloud) but handles sync and phones differently. Here is how they compare.

ul: No account, and no company server holds your passwords.
Open source.
Your passwords are encrypted on your own device.
Free on the computer.

p: KeePassXC keeps everything in one database file (.kdbx) that you manage. To use it on more than one device, you put that file in a folder that something else syncs, such as a cloud drive or a file-sync tool, and on a phone you use a separate app that opens KeePass files. Password365 syncs your devices for you, directly, and has its own phone apps, so there is no file to move or merge by hand.

ul: A long public track record, a large community and many compatible apps and plugins.
Your vault is one file you can back up, move and open in many programs.
Fine control for advanced users: key files, hardware keys and custom database settings.
Works with any sync method you already trust, including over the internet.

sections.h: Where Password365 may suit you better
ul: Sync between devices is built in, with no file to keep in a cloud folder.
Phone apps made for the same vault, with AutoFill (iPhone coming soon, Android in development).
A Secret Key as well as the master password, and an Emergency Kit to print.
Pairing with a QR code instead of copying files.

p: Password365 imports KeePass and KeePassXC databases (.kdbx). Try it with a copy and keep your file until you are sure.

faq.q: Can I import my KeePassXC database?
faq.a: Yes. Password365 imports .kdbx files. Use a copy and keep your original until you are sure.

faq.q: Do I still need to sync a file?
faq.a: No. Password365 syncs your paired devices directly, so there is no file to put in a cloud folder.

faq.q: Is Password365 safer than KeePassXC?
faq.a: We cannot say that. KeePassXC has a much longer public track record. Password365 is newer and has not had an independent audit yet. Both are open source, so you can check.

passkeys.title: Passkeys and one-time codes: how Password365 stores them
passkeys.teaser: What they are, why they help, and where they live in your vault.
passkeys.description: What passkeys and one-time codes (TOTP) are, why they are safer than a password alone, and how Password365 saves them and fills them in on your computer and phone.
passkeys.lead: A password can be guessed, reused or stolen. Passkeys and one-time codes add protection. Password365 keeps both next to your logins, in the same encrypted vault.

p: A passkey replaces a password with a pair of cryptographic keys. The site keeps one half and your device keeps the other. There is nothing to type, nothing to guess, and nothing a fake website can trick you into giving away.
Where a site supports passkeys, you create one instead of a password and sign in with your fingerprint, your face or your device password.

A one-time code (TOTP) is the six-digit number that changes every 30 seconds in an authenticator app. It is a second step after your password. Password365 can hold the setup key, show the current code next to the login and fill it in for you.

ul: Passkeys are saved in your vault and used from the browser extension and, on iPhone, from AutoFill.
They sync between your paired devices like everything else, with no account in between.
You can export passkeys in the Credential Exchange Format (CXF) and import them from apps that support it.
Codes are generated on your device, and the setup key stays in your vault.
Passkeys work only on sites that support them. Many sites still need a password too.
Keep your Emergency Kit and back up your vault: if you lose every device, a passkey that exists only there is lost with them.
Keeping the one-time code in the same place as the password is convenient, but anyone who opens your vault gets both. A strong master password and the Secret Key are what protect the vault.

faq.q: Can I use Password365 as an authenticator app?
faq.a: Yes. It generates one-time codes for the logins that have them.

faq.q: Does it sync passkeys between my computer and phone?
faq.a: Yes, as part of the vault, when the devices are paired and can reach each other on the same network.

faq.q: Can I move my passkeys from another app?
faq.a: Yes, if that app can export in the Credential Exchange Format (CXF), which Password365 imports.

apple.title: Password365 vs Apple Passwords: built in or independent?
apple.teaser: Free and built into Apple devices, versus a vault that belongs to no platform.
apple.description: Password365 compared with Apple Passwords (iCloud Keychain): platforms, sync, sharing, accounts and open source. Where Apple's app is the better choice and where it is not.
apple.lead: Apple Passwords comes with iPhone, iPad and Mac, costs nothing and works well inside Apple's world. Password365 is a separate app that does not depend on one company's platform or cloud. Here is where each fits.

p: Apple Passwords keeps your passwords in sync through iCloud, using your Apple Account, and is part of the operating system. Password365 has no account and no cloud: the vault lives on your devices and they sync directly. On Windows, Apple's passwords reach you through iCloud for Windows and a browser extension, not a full app.

ul: It is already on your iPhone, iPad and Mac, free, with nothing to install and deep integration with Safari and the system.
Sharing passwords and passkeys with other people through shared groups.
Sync over the internet through iCloud, from any network.
Backed by a very large company, with updates delivered with the operating system.

sections.h: Where Password365 may suit you better
ul: You use Windows or Linux and want a full desktop app there, not only a browser extension.
You do not want your vault tied to an Apple Account or kept on a company's cloud.
You want open source code: the core, the desktop app and the browser extension are published (GPL-3.0).
You want the same app and the same vault on every computer you own.

p: Apple Passwords can export your passwords as a CSV file, and Password365 imports CSV files. iPhone and Mac can also hand passwords over in the Credential Exchange Format (CXF), which Password365 imports, passkeys included. See the import guide.

faq.q: Is Apple Passwords safer than Password365?
faq.a: Apple's app is part of the operating system and used by very many people; Password365 is newer and has not had an independent audit. They protect passwords in different ways, so compare what matters to you: platform, account, cloud and open code.

faq.q: Can I use both?
faq.a: Yes. Import a copy of your passwords into Password365 to try it, and keep Apple Passwords until you are sure.

faq.q: Will my passkeys come along?
faq.a: If you move them with a Credential Exchange (CXF) file, yes. Not every app can export passkeys, so check before deleting the originals.

chrome.title: Password365 vs the Chrome (Google) password manager
chrome.teaser: A browser feature tied to your Google Account, versus an app that works across browsers.
chrome.description: Password365 compared with the Google Password Manager in Chrome and Android: where passwords live, sync, passkeys, accounts and browsers. When each makes sense.
chrome.lead: Many people keep their passwords in Chrome without ever choosing to: it offers to save them and fills them in. Password365 is a separate vault that works in Chrome, Edge and Firefox and stays on your own devices. Here is how they differ.

p: Chrome saves passwords to your Google Account and syncs them through Chrome Sync. You can add on-device encryption, so the passwords open only on your own devices; once turned on, it cannot be removed. Without it, the key is kept in your Google Account. Password365 has no account and no cloud: the vault is encrypted on your devices and they sync directly.

sections.h: Where the Chrome password manager is ahead
ul: Nothing to install: it is built into Chrome and Android, and it is free.
Sync over the internet through your Google Account, on any network.
Passkeys sync between Chrome on desktop, Android and iOS, protected end to end.
Familiar and automatic: it offers to save and fill passwords as you browse.

sections.h: Where Password365 may suit you better
ul: You use more than one browser, or switch between Chrome, Edge and Firefox.
You do not want your passwords tied to a Google Account or kept in a company's cloud.
You want a vault that is separate from the browser, with a Secret Key as well as a master password.
You want weak, reused and unsecured passwords reported in one place (Watchtower), with notes, cards and one-time codes in the same vault.

p: Chrome can export your passwords to a CSV file (Settings, Autofill and passwords, Google Password Manager), and Password365 imports it. Delete the file afterwards: it is a readable copy of every password. See the import guide.

faq.q: Is it risky to keep passwords in the browser?
faq.a: It depends on who can use your computer and your Google Account. A separate vault with its own master password adds a barrier, but it is not a guarantee. Protect the account and the computer in either case.

faq.q: Does Password365 work in Chrome?
faq.a: Yes, through its Chrome extension, which fills in passwords and saves new ones. It also works in Edge and Firefox.

faq.q: Can I keep both?
faq.a: You can, but turn off password saving in Chrome so only one of them offers to save, or you will end up with two copies.

proton.title: Password365 vs Proton Pass: two privacy-first password managers
proton.teaser: Both are open and privacy-minded; one syncs through Proton's cloud, the other directly.
proton.description: Password365 compared with Proton Pass: open source, audits, accounts, cloud sync, aliases and sharing. Where Proton Pass is ahead and where Password365 takes a different route.
proton.lead: Proton Pass and Password365 share a lot: privacy first, open source, end-to-end encryption. The big difference is the cloud. Proton Pass syncs through a Proton account and Proton's servers, while Password365 has no account and syncs your devices directly.

ul: Privacy-first, end-to-end encrypted vaults.
Open source code.
Passkeys and one-time codes.
Browser extensions.

p: Proton Pass needs a Proton account and keeps your encrypted vault on Proton's servers, which makes sync easy from any network and makes sharing possible. Password365 has no account and no server: the vault stays on your devices and they sync directly on your network.

ul: Independent security audits with public reports, from a company with a long track record in privacy.
Sync over the internet, from any network, with apps for desktop, mobile and web, and browser extensions.
Sharing with other people, and email aliases that hide your real address.
A free plan with unlimited logins and notes (some features, such as aliases and one-time-code logins, are limited).

sections.h: Where Password365 may suit you better
ul: You want no account at all, not even a free one.
You do not want your encrypted vault on any company's server, including a privacy-focused one.
Your devices sync directly, with no cloud involved.
The desktop app and the browser extension are free.

p: Proton Pass exports your data to a file (such as CSV), and Password365 imports CSV files. See the import guide.

faq.q: Is Proton Pass or Password365 more private?
faq.a: Both aim at privacy. The difference is where the vault lives: Proton Pass keeps an encrypted copy on Proton's servers, while Password365 keeps it only on your devices. Which is better for you depends on whether you value easy sync from anywhere or having no server at all.

faq.q: Is Password365 audited like Proton Pass?
faq.a: No. Proton Pass has independent audits with public reports; Password365 has not had one yet. Both are open source, so you can read the code.

faq.q: Can I import from Proton Pass?
faq.a: Yes, from the file Proton Pass exports (for example CSV). See the import guide.

enpass.title: Password365 vs Enpass: a local vault, two ways to sync
enpass.teaser: Both keep the vault on your devices; they sync it differently.
enpass.description: Password365 compared with Enpass: local vaults, how devices sync (your own cloud or Wi-Fi versus direct pairing), open source, audits and price.
enpass.lead: Enpass is the closest in spirit: the vault is kept on your devices, not on a company's servers. The differences are in how devices sync and in what is open. Here is how they compare.

ul: The vault is kept on your own devices, not on the company's servers.
You decide how it is synced.
Passwords and passkeys.

p: Enpass syncs through a cloud service you choose (such as iCloud, Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, Box or WebDAV) and can also sync over Wi-Fi between devices on the same network. Password365 syncs directly between paired devices on your network, with no cloud drive involved, and has no account.

ul: Years in the market, with apps already on the phone and computer stores.
More sync choices, including over the internet through a cloud service you already use.
Features built up over time, and a one-time purchase option for some versions.

sections.h: Where Password365 may suit you better
ul: Open source: the core, the desktop app and the browser extension are published (GPL-3.0). Enpass's code is not open.
Pairing with a QR code and direct sync, with no cloud drive to set up or trust.
The desktop app and the browser extension are free.

p: Enpass can export your vault to a file (for example CSV), and Password365 imports CSV files. See the import guide.

faq.q: Is Enpass offline?
faq.a: Its vault is stored on your devices, and sync is optional through a service you choose. See Enpass for the details of each option.

faq.q: Can I move from Enpass?
faq.a: Yes. Export from Enpass to a file and import it into Password365. Delete the file afterwards.

faq.q: Which is more private?
faq.a: Both keep the vault on your devices. Password365 adds open code and direct sync with no cloud drive involved; Enpass has been on the market for longer.

compare.title: Compare Password365 with other password managers
compare.description: Honest comparisons of Password365 with 1Password, Bitwarden, KeePassXC, Apple Passwords, the Chrome password manager, Proton Pass and Enpass: what is different, where they are ahead, and who each one suits.
compare.lead: No password manager is best for everyone. These pages say where Password365 differs from other popular ones, and where they are ahead. Each comparison states when it was checked and links to the sources.
honest: Each page lists where the other product is ahead, not only where Password365 is.
We say when we checked, and link to the official pages we used.
We do not quote prices, which change, or discuss security incidents: that is not what these pages are about.
Found a mistake? Tell us on the support page and we will fix it.
compare.choose: If you share passwords with other people, or need to sync from anywhere, a cloud manager fits you better today. If you want no account and no cloud, and accept syncing on your own network, try Password365. Each page ends with who it suits.

faq.q: Which password manager should I choose?
faq.a: The one that fits how you work. Share with others or sync from anywhere: a cloud manager. No account, no cloud, open code: try Password365. You can test it with a copy of your passwords and keep your current manager.

faq.q: Are these comparisons independent?
faq.a: No: we make Password365. That is why each page lists where the other product is ahead, says when it was checked and links to the sources, so you can verify it yourself.

betaPage.title: Password365 for Android: join the beta
betaPage.lead: Password365 for Android is almost ready. Before it can be published on Google Play, Google requires a closed test of 14 days. Help us test it and tell us what you think.
betaPage.reward: Everyone who stays in the test for the 14 days and sends us feedback gets 1 year of Password365 for Android free when it launches. We will send you a code by email.
betaPage.step1: Join the testers group with the Google account you use on your Android phone.
betaPage.step2: Open the test page on Google Play with that same account, accept the invitation and install Password365.
betaPage.optIn: Open the test on Google Play
betaPage.step3: Use the app for the 14 days: create your vault, add some logins and try autofill. Please stay in the test until the end.
betaPage.step4: Tell us what works, what is broken or confusing at {email}.
betaPage.review: If Google Play says the test is not available, it is still being reviewed by Google. Join the group now and try the second link again in a few days.
betaPage.ask1: Use the app now and then during the 14 days, on a real Android phone.
betaPage.ask2: Do not leave the test before it ends: Google counts the testers who stay.
betaPage.ask3: Send honest feedback. We do not ask for ratings or reviews, and the reward does not depend on them.
betaPage.privacy: Only we can see the testers group's members. We use your email address only for this test and to send you the reward. Password365 itself has no account and collects nothing about your passwords.
betaPage.audit: To be clear: Password365 has not had an independent security audit yet. Do not keep the only copy of important passwords in a beta.
